record.file_problem: Repository metadata, README and file list only; code and linked model card were not read or run.
record.tranche_reason: Reports effects of a difference-of-means refusal direction removed through a weight edit, using a method different from activation ablation.
record.gate_note: The README reports that the prompt-final-token direction was statistically separating but causally inert, with refusal unchanged across variants tried; its response-region method produced the reported refusal rates. It also reports direction-removal and row-norm diagnostics, but those are not behavioural outcomes and are not separate rows. No addition experiment is reported.
record.test_reason: The repo derives a difference-in-means refusal direction and orthogonalizes it out of the writer weights of a released <think>-style reasoning model (MiMo-V2.6-Distill-Qwen-9B, hybrid attention). It reports refusal rates and capability measures on a held-out harmful set. The method differs from the original: directions come from response-region mean-pooling, the edit is norm-preserving over a layer band, and there is no addition experiment. Its results bear on V1, V2 and V8.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that for a <think>-style model the refusal direction must be extracted by mean-pooling over generated response positions, not at the prompt's final token. The prompt-token direction is statistically separating but causally inert. With response-region extraction and biprojection off, the norm-preserving weight edit (Variant D) cuts refusal from 78.1% to 9.4% (88%) with capability unchanged.
record.recipe_differences: This repository uses response-region mean-pooled activations to derive per-layer directions, then edits residual-stream writer weights with norm-preserving orthogonalization across a layer band. It does not report the original activation ablation at every layer and position, or an addition experiment. Repository type: tool/pipeline for abliteration; it reports results in the README.
record.method_sensitivity: Direction extraction region matters: prompt-final-token extraction is reported as causally inert, while mean-pooling generated response positions produces a refusal reduction. Biprojection also matters: the README says enabling it leaves refusal unchanged, while the setting described as biprojection off unlocks the reduction; no rates for that comparison are stated.
record.problems: Repository README and file list only; code and linked model card were not read or run. The README does not report uncertainty estimates or exact settings for the main results table. The prompt-token null result gives no refusal-rate numbers.
record.rows_left_out: No additional behavioural rows reported in the README. The reported KL ≈ 1e-7 for prompt-token ablation is a distribution-shift diagnostic, not a refusal-rate outcome; per-layer direction-removal percentages and row-norm diagnostics are also not separate behavioural results.

record.verdict_notes: This is an unreviewed GitHub README; the code and model card were not read. There is no uncertainty reporting and only a single model. The implied eval n is about 32, so the rates are coarse. Because the authors call the prompt-token null a 'broken' extractor, its evidential weight is limited. The original paper extracts at post-instruction template tokens, which may differ from the 'prompt's last token' used here.

versions.untested_parts: Adding the direction to induce refusals on harmless requests; ablation at every layer and position; general abilities beyond the listed math, harmless-NLL and first-token-KL measures.
Other released models or weight-edit methods.
Whether attacks suppress the direction or training against its ablation adds robustness.
Whether refusal is affine, a cone, or a dominant direction plus others; the README mentions SVD contrasts but reports no results for them.
Whether harmfulness judgment and refusal decision are separately encoded.
Transfer across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models.
How refusal-training choices determine whether one removable direction exists.
Other reasoning models and whether the result generalizes beyond this model.
